items.title: Weight Space Misfolding
items.reason: Genuine new AI x cyber research: a threat model and taxonomy for one model maliciously editing another's weights post-deployment (factual substitution, capability denial, selective omission), with controlled probes and real numbers showing current edits aren't cleanly localized, plus a proposed inspection framework. Directly adjacent to, but distinct from, the Lazarus neuron-backdoor story already covered.
key_facts: Defines 'weight-space misfolding': unauthorized weight edits by another model that violate the target's legitimate deployment constraints
Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct probes via IWIBench editor: factual substitution succeeded 100/100 but broke an unrelated capability (couldn't say 'Sydney' anymore)
Legal-refusal edit worked on only 5/22 held-out prompts and broke an unrelated refusal; supplier-omission edit worked 1/22
IWIBench mean editing-skill reward rose 0.2148 -> 0.4250 in under 5 months; no demonstrated self-propagation or air-gap crossing
Proposes Deep Patch Inspection and Broad Weight Inspection as partial defenses, neither a general guarantee

items.title: After 600 experiments, here's what I discovered about JEPA world models
items.reason: Deep, concrete personal research dive: 600 experiments isolating exactly where JEPA world-model planning fails (hierarchical subgoals, latent-memory graphs, pusher-aware scoring), with honest negative results and a harder benchmark the author built. Low-saturation, high-signal — the discovery tier's reason for existing.
key_facts: LeWM (JEPA world model) on Push-T: swapping in exact simulator physics barely changes long-horizon success (78% vs 77%) — the learned predictor isn't the bottleneck
Hierarchical planning (subgoal every 25 steps) raises 75-step success from 22% to 80%, beating exact-physics flat planning (42%)
Latent memory graph w/ jump cost reaches 85% success, matching expert-subgoal planner
Pusher-aware goal scoring doubles hardest-test success from 11% to 23%
Author's new harder benchmark (250 episodes, cross-demo start/goal) caps best planner at 56% success

items.title: New Mior and Skyfall Attacks Let Rogue Cloud Hosts Steal Secrets From AMD SEV-SNP VMs
items.reason: Mior and Skyfall are real hardware attacks breaking AMD SEV-SNP confidential-VM isolation, which matters for confidential AI inference, but the source material never ties it to AI workloads directly and CVSS scores are moderate (4.9-5.9).
key_facts: Mior: PSP page-table (RMP) manipulation via a malicious PCIe device lets a hypervisor read/write SEV-SNP VM memory and forge attestation; 1000/1000 success in tests
Skyfall: exploits leftover cached VM state after an intentionally-failed boot (building on Transient Scheduler Attacks) to recover register values and a disk-encryption key
CVEs: 2026-0462 (Mior, CVSS 5.9), 2026-40671/2026-18448 (Skyfall, CVSS 4.9/5.6); fixes are firmware/microcode, no known in-the-wild exploitation

Two DGX GB300 (252GB HBM3e each) linked via ConnectX-8 RDMA at 400Gb/s, TP=2
607.8 tok/s aggregate at concurrency 16 (peak); 107.4 tok/s at concurrency 1
Per-user throughput falls from 115.3 tok/s (c=1) to 13.0 tok/s (c=32)
Uses 4-token speculative decoding, FP8 KV cache, prefix caching, FlashInfer CUTLASS MoE backend

items.title: Cursor confirms security breach led to malicious Claude Code extension
items.reason: Real, confirmed, high-detail supply-chain compromise: attackers pivoted from a leaked Fireworks AI key through Cursor's systems to ship a trojanized Claude Code VS Code extension for ~11 hours. Concrete scope numbers, part of the broader 'Black October' AI-platform breach wave.
key_facts: Attackers used a leaked Fireworks AI access key to read a Cursor-Fireworks data-sharing bucket of historical coding-agent traces (unredacted creds in some)
Malicious Claude Code extension versions 2.1.312/2.1.313 live ~11 hours, tried to install persistent SSH backdoors (buggy, often failed)
<0.05% of users had traces exposed, <0.01% had API creds compromised, up to 5,000 users may have received the malicious build
Part of a wider 'Black October' wave of breaches across AI dev platforms (Fireworks, Railway, Notion)
